title: bedsharing_ms_v7
research_questions: To examine whether postconceptional age (PCA), the sum of gestational and postnatal age, clarifies how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to SUID incidence.
To determine the stability of the PCA window boundary diagnostics for at least 5 cases per week in each subgroup.
To compare incidence rate ratios between primary and sensitivity analyses restricting the PCA window to different durations.
data_sources_used: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) National Vital Statistics System linked birth records

variables.operationalization: PCA = gestational age at birth + postnatal age at death in completed weeks.
variables.quote: We analyzed 13,013 SUID cases (2008–2019) from the National Center for Fatality Review and Prevention Case Reporting System, modeling incidence across PCA with population-adjusted negative binomial regression.

variables.operationalization: Case-level bed sharing was classified from NCFRP death-scene sleep-environment variables rather than from PRAMS. Direct evidence of same-surface sharing was retained as bed sharing.
variables.quote: Bed sharing and infant sex were treated as non-imputable ground-truth variables; cases missing either (20 for sex, 1,467 for bed-sharing status) were excluded rather than assigned an inferred value.

variables.operationalization: Maternal smoking during pregnancy was derived from multiple NCFRP pregnancy smoking fields, including smoking before pregnancy, smoking at any time during pregnancy, and trimester-specific cigarette-use variables.
variables.quote: Infants were classified as smoke-exposed if maternal smoking was recorded before pregnancy or during any trimester, unexposed if available smoking fields consistently indicated no exposure, and unknown otherwise.

variables.operationalization: Preterm birth was defined as gestational age at birth less than 37 completed weeks.
variables.quote: Preterm birth was defined as gestational age at birth less than 37 completed weeks.

variables.operationalization: Cases were restricted to deaths classified as sudden infant death syndrome in the NCFRP database. Analyses were limited to infants who died within the first year of life.

claims.statement: Postconceptional age (PCA) may clarify how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to Sudden Unexpected Infant Death (SUID) incidence.
claims.quote: We examined whether postconceptional age (PCA), the sum of gestational and postnatal age, clarifies how bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity relate to SUID incidence.

claims.statement: The study analyzed 13,013 SUID cases from the National Center for Fatality Review and Prevention Case Reporting System using population-adjusted negative binomial regression.
claims.quote: We analyzed 13,013 SUID cases (2008–2019) from the National Center for Fatality Review and Prevention Case Reporting System, modeling incidence across PCA with population-adjusted negative binomial regression.

claims.statement: Bed sharing was more strongly associated with SUID incidence in an early developmental window (PCA <43 weeks) compared to a later one (PCA ≥47 weeks).
claims.quote: Bed sharing was more strongly associated with incidence in an early developmental window (PCA <43 weeks; incidence rate ratio [IRR] 6.45, 95% CI 3.14–13.23) than a later one (PCA ≥47 weeks; IRR 2.10, 95% CI 1.70–2.58)

claims.statement: Maternal smoking and prematurity showed a similar pattern of association with SUID incidence as bed sharing, remaining positively associated throughout.
claims.quote: maternal smoking and prematurity showed the same pattern while remaining positively associated throughout.

claims.statement: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was further amplified by maternal smoking in a later developmental window (PCA ≥47 weeks).
claims.quote: Bed sharing’s association with incidence was further amplified by maternal smoking in the late window (interaction IRR 1.57, 95% CI 1.19–2.08)

claims.statement: Associations between SUID incidence and bed sharing, maternal smoking, and prematurity were similar in males and females.
claims.quote: associations were similar in males and females, indicating these effects are sex-independent.

claims.statement: The developmental timing of SUID incidence showed a clear rise-peak-decline pattern when aligned by postconceptional age (PCA).
claims.quote: PCA alignment produced a clear rise-peak-decline pattern.

claims.statement: Bed sharing was recorded for 59.5% of SUID cases, and these cases were more often associated with maternal smoking during pregnancy (52.2%) compared to non-bed-sharing cases (40.8%).
claims.quote: Bed sharing was recorded for 7,739 cases (59.5%) and was absent for 5,274 (40.5%). Bed-sharing cases more often involved maternal smoking during pregnancy (52.2% versus 40.8%).

claims.statement: The incidence of SUID was highest in the first several months of life and then declined when analyzed on a postnatal age scale.
claims.quote: weekly incidence was highest in the first several months of life and then declined (Figure 2A)

claims.statement: When aligned by PCA, weekly SUID incidence followed a clearer developmental structure with a steep rise across early weeks, a peak in the mid-40-week range, and a gradual decline thereafter.
claims.quote: weekly incidence followed a clearer developmental structure, with a steep rise across the early weeks, a peak in the mid-40-week PCA range, and a gradual decline thereafter (Figure 2B)

claims.statement: Bed sharing was independently associated with higher incidence of SUID across both rising and declining phases of the developmental curve.
claims.quote: bed sharing remained strongly associated with higher incidence, although its magnitude was smaller than that of maternal smoking.

claims.statement: Maternal smoking during pregnancy showed the largest and most consistent association with SUID incidence in both windows.
claims.quote: maternal smoking during pregnancy showed the largest and most consistent association with SUID incidence in both windows

claims.statement: Prematurity remained a positive and significant correlate of SUID incidence across the developmental window, though roughly twice as strong early as late.
claims.quote: prematurity remained a positive and significant correlate across the developmental window, though roughly twice as strong early as late

claims.statement: The association between bed sharing and SUID incidence was larger among smokers (IRR 3.35) than non-smokers (IRR 2.07) in the later developmental window.
claims.quote: the late-window bed-sharing association among smokers (IRR 3.35) than non-smokers (IRR 2.07)

claims.statement: The developmental structure of risk was similar in girls and boys once bed sharing, smoking, and prematurity were explicitly modeled.
claims.quote: the developmental structure of risk was similar in girls and boys.

claims.statement: PCA alignment resolved heterogeneity and yielded a smooth rise-peak-decline incidence curve, consistent with a single underlying developmental process.
claims.quote: Aligning by PCA resolves this heterogeneity and yields a smooth, roughly symmetric rise-peak-decline incidence curve

claims.statement: The study is an observational analysis of registry-based case data, resulting in associative rather than causal estimates.
claims.quote: this was an observational analysis of registry-based case data, and the resulting estimates are associative rather than causal.

claims.statement: Sleep-environment classification in case-report systems may be subject to heterogeneity in ascertainment and reporting.
claims.quote: sleep-environment classification in case-report systems may be subject to heterogeneity in ascertainment and reporting.

claims.statement: The bed-sharing denominator was derived indirectly from external prevalence estimates rather than a source linked to the cases.
claims.quote: the bed-sharing denominator was derived indirectly from external prevalence estimates rather than a source linked to the cases

claims.statement: The analytic strategy excluded sparse strata and zero-count cells, meaning the fitted models describe observed high-information strata rather than a fully enumerated population lattice.
claims.quote: the analytic strategy intentionally excluded sparse strata and zero-count cells to stabilize estimation

claims.statement: The peak interval was treated descriptively rather than modeled directly in the windowed regressions due to week-to-week instability.
claims.quote: the peak interval was treated descriptively rather than modeled directly in the windowed regressions because of week-to-week instability

claims.statement: The exposure IRRs, particularly maternal smoking IRR, are not directly comparable in magnitude to case-control effect estimates.
claims.quote: the exposure IRRs, and the maternal smoking IRR in particular, are not directly comparable in magnitude to case-control effect estimates

claims.statement: The largest single exclusion was missing or invalid maternal smoking status (6,113 cases), which were excluded rather than imputed.
claims.quote: these cases were excluded rather than imputed, which assumes that smoking-status missingness is unrelated to the outcome within the observed cohort

claims.statement: The case series should be understood as a large, growing multi-jurisdiction surveillance sample rather than a fixed national census.
claims.quote: the case series should be understood as a large, growing multi-jurisdiction surveillance sample rather than a fixed national census

claims.statement: The absolute incidence scale shown in Figure 2 is a population proxy rather than a jurisdiction-matched rate.
claims.quote: the absolute incidence scale shown in Figure 2 is a population proxy rather than a jurisdiction-matched rate

claims.statement: The split between suffocation and undetermined codes reflects diagnostic-practice-dependent ascertainment patterns.
claims.quote: the split between suffocation and undetermined codes is diagnostic-practice-dependent and can vary by jurisdiction and year

claims.statement: The study does not provide fine-grained mechanistic claims about the pathway from bed sharing to death.
claims.quote: no fine-grained mechanistic claim about the pathway from bed sharing to death is made here

claims.statement: The manuscript specifies a PCA window of 36 to 90 weeks and checks it against a count-stability criterion.
claims.quote: Prespecified PCA window (36-90 weeks) checked against a count-stability criterion of at least 5 cases per week in each of 4 tracked subgroups

claims.statement: The manuscript includes a sensitivity analysis comparing the primary PCA window (36-90 weeks) with an upper-bound restriction to 79 weeks.
claims.quote: Late-window incidence rate ratios at the primary PCA window (36-90 weeks) versus an upper-bound sensitivity analysis restricting the window to PCA 36-79 weeks

claims.statement: The manuscript presents interaction terms from windowed negative binomial models for bed sharing by maternal smoking and preterm birth.
